One test can use up to about %1$d MB of your data plan.
Results are stored in the session with the server URL and the radio values of the same seconds. A test during a traffic capture is flagged, because the capture slows it down.
The main target. Use a server you control, so results stay comparable between tests and days. For a LibreSpeed server, enter its address and tap Fill; any other web server works with three URLs.
Answers small requests quickly, e.g. an empty page.
Serves a large file (tens of MB or more); requested again until the time is up.
Accepts POST requests and throws the data away.
Plain HTTP to %1$s is not allowed in this build, so the test would fail. Use https://, or ask whoever builds the app to allow this host (netlogger.cleartextHosts).
Saved. The Live screen shows \"Run speed test (my server)\" while logging.
No server saved yet: the speed test is off.

Optional, for comparison only. Adds a second button on the Live screen that tests against %1$s. Not your server and never the default: the result depends on Cloudflare\'s nearest site and its route, and many large tests in a row are blocked for a while (HTTP 429). Each result stores the URL it used.
Start and stop it on the Live screen while a session is logging. One capture per session; it stops when the session stops.
NetLogger runs its own VPN on the phone. Android asks you once to allow it. Only one VPN can run at a time, so turn off any other VPN first.

It records the IP traffic between each app and the VPN, and which app owns each connection. It does not see radio signalling, and packet sizes and timing are rebuilt by the VPN, not the ones on the air.
The session export adds capture.pcap (open it in Wireshark), capture_sync.csv (clock alignment with the radio log) and connections.csv (the app of each connection).
Files grow with the traffic: a speed test during a capture adds about 100 MB to the pcap. Speed tests during a capture are flagged, because the capture slows them down.
Applies to the next capture. Traffic of apps not chosen bypasses the VPN and is not recorded.
Everything the phone sends and receives, including background apps and system services.
Only the apps you tick below, e.g. one video app for a QoE test. Smaller files that are easier to analyse.
No app selected yet: until you tick one, all apps are captured.
Only apps with an icon in the app drawer are listed. Include NetLogger itself to capture its speed tests.
The largest packet the VPN passes on. Applies to the next capture; the value is stored with it.
The same packet sizes as on a mobile network, so the pcap looks like real traffic. Fast links lose up to a quarter of their download speed during the capture.
Hardly slows the phone down (about 3 percent), but packets are bigger than on the air. Use it when throughput matters more than packet sizes.

Phones differ in which radio values Android gives to apps: some hide them, some report them only now and then. This page reads 3 cell updates (about 2 seconds) and shows what came back. Values that need 5G coverage are marked as such, not as missing. Below each field: how often it had a value in the sessions recorded on this phone, which is more reliable than one check.
Checked at %1$s. Copy report puts this page on the clipboard as text.
Stored with every session, so results can be compared between phones.
Red means it stops or weakens a test.
Yes: speed tests are refused, and the phone may not use 5G
Yes: a traffic capture cannot start unless it is NetLogger\'s own
Optimised: Android may slow logging with the screen off
Available: the phone gives the value. Limited: only partly, or worked out by NetLogger. Missing: the phone does not give it now.
The recorded sessions could not be counted.
Recorded sessions: no rows with this kind of cell yet
Recorded sessions: not stored per row, so only the live check shows it
Received power of the cell\'s reference signal; the main coverage measure.
Signal quality, including interference and load.
Signal to noise; the scale differs between phone makers.
Total received power on the channel.
Channel quality the phone reports to the network; many phones give it only while data flows.
A rough distance to the cell; often only while data flows.
Physical cell ID; changes show handovers.
The channel number; gives the frequency.
From the phone (API) or worked out by NetLogger from the channel number (mapped).
Cell ID and tracking area code; identify the site.
Many phones list no 5G cell in NSA mode; then PCI, channel and band are missing.
The second source of 5G values, used when the cell list has none.
Received power of the 5G synchronisation signal; the main 5G coverage measure.
Power of the 5G channel state reference signal; few phones report it.
5G physical cell ID; only from the cell list.
5G channel number; only from the cell list.
Bandwidth of each carrier in use; more than one means carrier aggregation.
Other cells the phone hears; needed to study handovers. The number is the most seen in this check.
Whether Android answered the request for new cell data in time; otherwise NetLogger falls back to older data.
